fenwick-tree-intro.introduction: A Binary Indexed Tree (BIT) or Fenwick Tree is a data structure that can efficiently update elements and calculate prefix sums in a table of numbers.
fenwick-tree-intro.intuition: Every integer can be represented as sum of powers of two (its binary representation). A BIT stores partial sums based on these powers of two. We can navigate these ranges by adding or subtracting the Least Significant Bit (LSB).

walkthrough.description: The Least Significant Bit of `i` can be extracted using `i & (-i)`.
To add `val` at index `i`, we update `tree[i]`, then move to `i = i + (i & (-i))` to update all ranges that encompass `i`.
To get sum from 1 to `i`, we add `tree[i]` to our sum, then move to `i = i - (i & (-i))` to get the sum of the preceding range.

steps: Query(3): sum += tree[3]. Next i = 3 - (3 & -3) = 2. sum += tree[2]. Next i = 2 - (2 & -2) = 0. Stop.

complexities.analysis: Both update and query jump through set bits, which can be at most log(N).

mistakes: Using 0-based indexing for the tree array. BIT requires 1-based indexing because `0 & -0` is 0, which causes an infinite loop in the update/query functions.
tips: Always use BIT over Segment Tree if you only need Prefix Sums and Point Updates. It is much faster in practice and requires 4x less memory.

count-inversions.introduction: Given an array, an inversion is a pair `(i, j)` where `i < j` and `arr[i] > arr[j]`. Find the total number of inversions.
count-inversions.intuition: If we iterate from right to left, we want to know how many elements we've seen so far that are smaller than the current element. A Fenwick Tree can keep a running frequency count of elements seen.

walkthrough.description: If array elements are large or negative, compress them to ranks 1 to N.
Loop from the end of the array to the start.
Query the BIT for sum of frequencies from 1 to `arr[i]-1`. Add this to total inversions. Then, Add(arr[i], 1) to the BIT.

complexities.analysis: For each of the N elements, we do a Query O(log N) and an Add O(log N).

mistakes: Forgetting Coordinate Compression. If an element in the array is 10^9, you can't create a BIT of size 10^9. You must map the values to 1...N.
tips: Merge Sort is the standard algorithm for this problem, but the BIT approach is extremely elegant and often easier to write in an interview once you know the BIT template.
